title: Teacher Transformation: The Two Things It Takes
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Reflecting on a summer of traveling to schools across seven states for PD work, Stuart identifies what a genuinely transformative professional-development experience requires: renewal of the mind and action with the body. He argues that PD itself cannot transform a teacher -- the teacher must do the work, just as his own students must do the work of learning with care -- but that his job as a PD facilitator is still to make transformation as achievable as possible. He describes how thinking tools like the Credibility CCP, the Rainbow of Why, the Effort/Efficacy Flywheel, and the Five Key Beliefs Pyramid function as "graphic organizers for fundamental truths," gradually renewing a teacher's mind through repeated attention. But mind renewal alone isn't enough; teachers must also put ideas into embodied practice, because watching videos and reading books without doing anything produces no change. Stuart closes by noting that the strongest transformation happens when specific practices reinforce the ideas a teacher is already renewing their mind with, turning theory from a burden into "a boon."
points: Stuart's two-part transformation model -- mind renewal plus embodied action -- puts the responsibility for change on the teacher, framing his own job as merely making that transformation "as straightforward as possible."
His suite of thinking tools are explicitly framed as "graphic organizers for fundamental truths about teaching and learning," not just decorative graphics.
He's blunt that consuming content isn't enough: watching videos and reading books without doing things won't produce transformation.

Real transformation compounds when a PD leader's recommended practices directly reinforce the mental models being taught, so the two halves -- renewed mind, embodied practice -- mutually reinforce each other over time.
quotes: What a good professional development endeavor does: it enables transformation. We don't come to PD hoping to leave entirely unchanged; at the same time, we don't come hoping to change everything.
Well, first, let's be clear: teacher PD can't transform a teacher. Rather, the teacher must do certain kinds of things, with care.
The human mind is constantly renewing itself — dismantling unused things, adopting new things, creating new neural pathways, overwriting old ones.
These aren't just pretty graphics or gimmicks; they are instead graphic organizers for fundamental truths about teaching and learning.
You can watch every YouTube video I've made and read every book I've written 100 times, but if you don't DO THINGS, you won't be transformed. Nor will I.
But theories are only burdensome things when they don't make sense in my mind and don't seem actionable with my body. When theories do meet these criteria, they are a boon.
